title: Imports and Namespace Setup
content: Imports Mathlib.Data.Nat.Squarefree for the Squarefree predicate, Finset.Basic for finite-set operations in Konyagin's bound, Order.Filter.Basic for the ∀ᶠ (eventually) quantifier used in asymptotic statements, and Tactic for automation.
mathContext: The `Squarefree` predicate from Mathlib defines $n$ is squarefree iff $\forall d, d^2 \mid n \Rightarrow d = 1$, equivalently $\mu(n) \ne 0$ where $\mu$ is the Möbius function. The `Filter.atTop` filter on $\mathbb{N}$ provides $\forall^\infty j$ meaning 'for all sufficiently large $j$'.

title: Squarefree Sumset
content: SquarefreeSumset A requires that a + b is squarefree for ALL a, b ∈ A (including a = b, so 2a must also be squarefree). This links additive structure to multiplicative constraints: for each prime p, the elements of A must avoid collisions modulo p², and these constraints interact across all primes simultaneously.
mathContext: Defines $\text{SquarefreeSumset}(A) :\equiv \forall a, b \in A,\, \text{Squarefree}(a + b)$. Since $a + b$ ranges over the sumset $A + A = \{a + b : a, b \in A\}$, this requires every element of $A + A$ to be squarefree. For each prime $p$, the condition $p^2 \nmid (a+b)$ means $a \not\equiv -b \pmod{p^2}$, eliminating roughly $1/p^2$ of pairs. The Chinese Remainder Theorem makes the constraints across different primes nearly independent, but their cumulative effect is severe: the set $A$ must be sparse.

title: Set Enumeration Axiom
content: Axiomatizes enumSet A j as the j-th smallest element of an infinite set A. The specification enumSet_spec guarantees StrictMono (enumSet A) and Set.range (enumSet A) = A, providing a canonical increasing enumeration. This avoids constructive well-ordering issues in Lean while enabling growth rate analysis.
mathContext: Axiomatizes a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfying: (1) $f$ is strictly monotone: $i < j \Rightarrow f(i) < f(j)$; (2) $\text{range}(f) = A$. For any infinite $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, such an $f$ exists uniquely — it is the order-preserving bijection $\mathbb{N} \xrightarrow{\sim} A$. We write $a_j = f(j)$ and ask: how fast must $a_j \to \infty$?

title: Exponential Growth Conjecture
content: ErdosProblem1103 states: for every infinite A with SquarefreeSumset, ∃ C > 1 such that C^j ≤ a_j for all sufficiently large j. Defined as a Prop (not axiom) since it is an open conjecture. Uses Filter.atTop for the 'eventually' quantifier and real-valued exponential comparison via C ^ (j : ℝ).
mathContext: States $\forall A \subseteq \mathbb{N},\, A \text{ infinite} \wedge \text{SquarefreeSumset}(A) \Rightarrow \exists C > 1,\, \forall^\infty j,\, C^j \le a_j$. Equivalently: $\liminf_{j \to \infty} (a_j)^{1/j} > 1$. The conjecture asserts exponential growth $a_j \ge C^j$ is unavoidable. The status is OPEN: the best lower bound is polynomial ($j^{4/3}$) and the best upper construction is subexponential ($\exp(5j/\log j)$).

title: Van Doorn–Tao Upper Bound (2025)
content: There EXISTS an infinite squarefree-sumset sequence with subexponential growth: a_j < exp(5j / log j) for large j. This is subexponential because 5j/log j = o(j), so exp(5j/log j) = o(C^j) for any C > 1. The construction uses careful selection of elements avoiding squarefree-sumset violations while maintaining controlled growth.
mathContext: Axiomatizes $\exists A \subseteq \mathbb{N},\, A \text{ infinite} \wedge \text{SquarefreeSumset}(A) \wedge \forall^\infty j,\, a_j < \exp\!\left(\frac{5j}{\log j}\right)$. The growth rate $\exp(5j/\log j)$ is superpolynomial (faster than any $j^k$) but subexponential (slower than any $C^j$ for $C > 1$). If the conjecture is true, this sequence must fail for large $j$; if false, slower-growing constructions may exist.

title: Van Doorn–Tao Lower Bound (2025)
content: ANY infinite squarefree-sumset sequence satisfies a_j > 0.24 · j^{4/3} for all j. The exponent 4/3 means the sequence grows at least as fast as j^{4/3}, ruling out slow polynomial growth. The proof uses sieve methods to bound how densely a squarefree-sumset can pack into intervals.
mathContext: Axiomatizes $\forall A,\, A \text{ infinite} \wedge \text{SquarefreeSumset}(A) \Rightarrow \forall j,\, 0.24 \cdot j^{4/3} < a_j$. The exponent $4/3$ arises from counting squarefree residues: in $[1, N]$, a squarefree-sumset can contain at most $O(N^{3/4})$ elements (inverse of $4/3$). The gap between this polynomial lower bound and the conjectured exponential lower bound is the heart of the problem.

title: Konyagin Finite Bound
content: For a FINITE set A ⊆ {1,…,N} with squarefree sumset, |A| ≤ C · N^{11/15}. The exponent 11/15 ≈ 0.733 means squarefree-sumsets are sparse but not extremely so — they can contain up to N^{0.733} out of N elements. Formalized with Finset, explicit constant C > 0, and the squarefree pairwise sum condition.
mathContext: Axiomatizes $\exists C > 0,\, \forall N,\, \forall A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,N\} \text{ (Finset)},\, \text{SquarefreeSumset}(A) \Rightarrow |A| \le C \cdot N^{11/15}$. The exponent $11/15$ comes from the large sieve for squarefree residues: the number of allowable residue classes modulo $p^2$ is $p^2 - \binom{k}{2}$ where $k$ is the set size, optimized over primes. Complementary to the infinite-sequence bounds.

title: Singleton Characterization
content: SquarefreeSumset {a} ↔ Squarefree (a + a): a singleton set satisfies the squarefree-sumset condition if and only if 2a is squarefree. Since the only pair is (a, a), the only sum to check is a + a = 2a. Axiomatized as the proof requires unfolding set membership.
mathContext:
States $	ext{SquarefreeSumset}(\{a\}) \iff 	ext{Squarefree}(2a)$. For $2a$ to be squarefree, we need $4 
mid 2a$, i.e., $a$ must be odd (since $2a$ already has factor $2$, squarefreeness requires $4 
mid 2a$). More generally, $p^2 
mid 2a$ for all primes $p$.

title: Empty Set is Squarefree-Sumset
content: SquarefreeSumset ∅ holds vacuously: there are no elements a ∈ ∅ to produce a pair, so the universal quantifier is trivially satisfied. Proved by introduction and contradiction via Set.not_mem_empty.
mathContext: Proves $\text{SquarefreeSumset}(\emptyset)$ by vacuous truth: $\forall a \in \emptyset, \ldots$ is true because $\emptyset$ has no elements. This is the base case for inductive constructions of squarefree-sumsets.

title: Subset Monotonicity
content: If SquarefreeSumset A and B ⊆ A, then SquarefreeSumset B. The squarefree-sumset property is hereditary: fewer elements means fewer sums to check, so the property can only be maintained or gained when passing to subsets.
mathContext: Proves $B \subseteq A \wedge \text{SquarefreeSumset}(A) \Rightarrow \text{SquarefreeSumset}(B)$. The proof is direct: for $a, b \in B$, we have $a, b \in A$ by $B \subseteq A$, so $\text{Squarefree}(a+b)$ by the hypothesis on $A$. This monotonicity is crucial: it means the family of squarefree-sumsets forms a downward-closed family (ideal) in the lattice of subsets.

title: 1 is Squarefree
content: The number 1 is squarefree, proved by invoking squarefree_one from Mathlib. This basic fact is used in constructions: any set containing 1 must have 1 + a squarefree for all other elements a.
mathContext: Proves $\text{Squarefree}(1)$: since $1$ has no prime factors, no $p^2$ can divide it. Equivalently, $\mu(1) = 1 \ne 0$. In the context of squarefree sumsets, including $1 \in A$ requires $1 + a$ to be squarefree for all $a \in A$, i.e., no $a \equiv -1 \pmod{p^2}$ for any prime $p$.
